OK, quick and dirty lesson on derivatives: They don't really exist. Somebody plugs a bunch of data about stocks into a computer, has it "guess" at a fit equation that matches the activity of the stocks, and gets winds up with a formula that appears to match the data (but is actually manufactured almost at random and has not even the slightest connection to anything that might actually affect the value of a stock). They then take the derivative of that formula. A derivative is just the rate of change, which for complex formulae is another equation, with different values at different places (or times). The upshot is, by setting the derivative to 0, that value is where the original formula will stop going up and start going down (or vice versa, but they don't generally pick stocks that are already failing). There are a few options on how to make money on this, but the upshot is that it almost always causes the stock to fail at the specified time. When large brokerages start selling off stock, others will follow, etc, and that's the most straightforward way it can happen. If they were just selling off stock to make that stock fail, that would be illegal, but since they are working off of a formula, even though that formula has no basis in reality, it's legal. As a person is either born or dies, there is a very short time period for the government to be notified of such and the number is either issued (in case of new births) or rescinded (in case of a death).   Based upon this one statistic, a stable money supply could be created.
